passage:
For forty-one years, Ida Brannock walked out to the white box on the schoolhouse lawn in Wendle Cross at nine each morning, read the two instruments inside, a rain gauge and a thermometer, and wrote both figures in a handwritten ledger begun in 1938. In all that time the record shows one gap: eleven blank lines one February, when a fall on the ice kept her in hospital. Her rule was that no other person's figures went into the ledger, so the lines stayed empty.

This spring, at seventy-eight, she stepped down as keeper, and the idea of a sensor was her own. Her letter to the district weather office at Lowmarch, asking for one to stand beside her box on trial, pointed to the eleven blank lines: her wish was that the record have no second gap after her. After a month of the trial, she wrote to the parish council.

At the meeting, Neve Callan, who teaches the older class at the village school, offered her pupils to take the nine o'clock reading in turns, and the office said it would take figures from either, since both had passed its checks. The council's chair said the vote rested on a single point: for a month, the machine's figures had matched Ida's to the tenth of a degree. The council voted for the sensor.

The sensor went up in April on a pole beside the white box. It sends its figures to Lowmarch every ten minutes, and its battery holds enough charge to run for a year. The handwritten ledger, nine volumes of it, went to the parish archive, its last line in Ida's hand.

Neve brought her class to watch that last reading, the last time anyone would cross the lawn to the box. Then the book was shut and carried to the archive, where the rest of its final page stays empty under Ida's last figure. The box still stands on the lawn with its door latched, and at nine each morning the children walk past it on their way into school.

passage:
For many summers Tamsin Rowe has led a July walk through the Hatherby cutting, where a railway once ran between an old platform and a brick footbridge. Volunteers with red torches walk it in about 16 minutes, marking each green light on a map. Rowe's first walk found 42, and the usual total is now about ninety. Last July the count fell to 23.

Every light is a wingless female glow-worm. What she needs from the cutting is a tall grass stem to climb after full dark, where she glows to draw flying males, and turf for her larvae, which feed on snails for two years before they become adults.

That had been a dry spring, and the cutting had changed. In March the Hatherby Line Trust put up 28 solar lamps at the platform end; in April it widened the path with gravel; in May its contractor did the mowing of the banks, usually left until September. Because the trust now locks the platform gate at ten, the walk had also moved an hour earlier, to half past nine. The trust's first step after the low count was to leave the gate open one night so the walk could be repeated at the old hour of half past ten.

That walk found much the same low total. Despite the dry spring, each of Rowe's 35 snail boards came up crowded, and her notebook held a page of tallies for every one. Under the lamps the banks had lost about as many lights as the dark stretch beyond them. The maps showed one clear line. A steep strip below the footbridge, beyond reach of the mowing, shone as thickly as ever right down to the new gravel, while the mown banks on either side were nearly bare.

The contractor, Joss Hebden, came to the next walk himself, on his knees at the steep strip with a red torch like everyone else. He has moved the mowing back to September, paid to reseed the bare banks out of his own pocket, and asked Rowe for a copy of her map, which he now keeps in his van.

passage:
The radio warned of frost at supper: minus four by dawn, with the apricots in full blossom. Tomas went out to the barn first to count the cans of oil: eleven, enough for the burners under half the orchard. Then he read the thermometer nailed to the gate, looked over the blossoms on the corner tree, the old tree his father had planted by the gate, and walked down to the young trees in the far row. Last, he looked across the lane at Mrs. Odell's orchard.

His plan was to keep every burner in a ring round the corner tree. It gave the best fruit on the place; his father had planted it, but it was the crop he thought of. I helped him set the burners out with care. The first flames drew moths out of the dark by the hundred.

Mrs. Odell came across the lane at eleven. She had judged the cold on that hillside for forty years, and she warned him that it would pool in the hollow, where his far row and her lowest trees stood side by side. She asked him to share the burners along the hollow and let the old tree take its chances, and offered to help. Tomas heard her out, thanked her, and kept to his plan. She went back and lit her own orchard with her own oil.

Near four the thermometer on the gate read minus three, but down in the hollow the frost was white on the grass. Inside the ring the corner tree stood bright, out of the cold's reach, and Tomas spent the night guarding it.

By morning the corner tree had come through and the far row was lost. Mrs. Odell's low trees, under her own burners, were saved. The radio put the next frost weeks away, past any need to light the burners again. Tomas said the forecast had been two degrees out, and sent me alone to count the dead trees while he raked under the corner tree. It had been Mrs. Odell, and not the radio, who had told him where the cold would go.
